::: {.lesson-meta}
Part 3 · Lesson 2 · About 60 minutes
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Analogy: ordering from a menu, not cooking"}
In Python you tell the computer *how* to do something, step by step: loop over the lines, check each one, collect the matches. **SQL** (Structured Query Language) is different: you describe *what* you want ("the open issues with more than one comment, most discussed first") and the database works out how to get it, like ordering a dish instead of cooking it. That difference is why a database can make your question fast without you changing it (lesson 3.6).
:::

## Tables, rows and columns

A **table** has named **columns**, each with a **type**, and holds **rows**. Unlike a spreadsheet, every value in a column must have that column's type, and the rules you declare are enforced on every write.

Connect to the practice database from lesson 3.1 (`docker compose exec db psql -U atlas -d practice`) and create a table:

```sql
CREATE TABLE issues (
    number      integer     PRIMARY KEY,
    repo        text        NOT NULL,
    title       text        NOT NULL,
    state       text        NOT NULL DEFAULT 'open',
    comments    integer     NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL
);
```

| Part | Means |
|---|---|
| `integer`, `text`, `timestamptz` | column types: whole numbers, text of any length, and a time-zone-aware timestamp (lesson 1.7's advice, enforced by the database) |
| `PRIMARY KEY` | this column uniquely identifies each row: no two rows may share it, and it can't be empty |
| `NOT NULL` | a value is required. `NULL` is SQL's "no value", like Python's `None` |
| `DEFAULT 'open'` | used when an insert doesn't provide a value |

SQL keywords aren't case-sensitive; writing them in capitals is a common convention that makes them stand out. Statements end with `;`. Text values use **single** quotes: `'open'`.

## INSERT: adding rows

```sql
INSERT INTO issues (number, repo, title, comments, created_at) VALUES
    (101, 'pytorch/ignite', 'Fix typo in Engine docstring',  2, '2026-11-02 09:14Z'),
    (102, 'pytorch/ignite', 'Add example for EarlyStopping', 5, '2026-10-20 15:00Z'),
    (103, 'pytorch/ignite', 'Support new metric: MAPE',      0, '2026-06-01 08:30Z'),
    (104, 'pytorch/vision', 'Clarify transforms docs',       1, '2026-11-10 12:00Z'),
    (105, 'pytorch/ignite', 'Flaky test in test_checkpoint', 8, '2025-12-24 18:45Z');
```
```text
INSERT 0 5
```

`state` wasn't listed, so every row got the default, `'open'`. (These issues are practice data.)

## SELECT: asking questions

```sql
SELECT * FROM issues;
```
```text
 number |      repo      |             title             | state | comments |       created_at
--------+----------------+-------------------------------+-------+----------+------------------------
    101 | pytorch/ignite | Fix typo in Engine docstring  | open  |        2 | 2026-11-02 09:14:00+00
    102 | pytorch/ignite | Add example for EarlyStopping | open  |        5 | 2026-10-20 15:00:00+00
    103 | pytorch/ignite | Support new metric: MAPE      | open  |        0 | 2026-06-01 08:30:00+00
    104 | pytorch/vision | Clarify transforms docs       | open  |        1 | 2026-11-10 12:00:00+00
    105 | pytorch/ignite | Flaky test in test_checkpoint | open  |        8 | 2025-12-24 18:45:00+00
(5 rows)
```

`*` means "every column". In real code, name the columns you need. A useful query picks columns, filters rows, and orders them:

```sql
SELECT number, title, comments
FROM issues
WHERE repo = 'pytorch/ignite' AND comments > 1
ORDER BY comments DESC;
```
```text
 number |             title             | comments
--------+-------------------------------+----------
    105 | Flaky test in test_checkpoint |        8
    102 | Add example for EarlyStopping |        5
    101 | Fix typo in Engine docstring  |        2
(3 rows)
```

Read it in the order the database thinks about it: **FROM** this table, keep rows **WHERE** the condition holds, **SELECT** these columns, **ORDER BY** this. `DESC` means descending (`ASC`, ascending, is the default). Without `ORDER BY`, rows come back in no guaranteed order, even if it looks consistent.

### Filtering

| Condition | Matches |
|---|---|
| `comments > 1`, `=`, `<>` (not equal), `<=` | comparisons |
| `AND`, `OR`, `NOT` | combine conditions |
| `title LIKE 'Fix%'` | text pattern: `%` is any run of characters, `_` one character |
| `title ILIKE '%doc%'` | the same, ignoring case (a Postgres extra) |
| `number IN (101, 104)` | one of a list |
| `created_at >= '2026-10-01'` | dates compare naturally |
| `deleted_at IS NULL` | no value. Never `= NULL`: nothing equals NULL, not even NULL |

```sql
SELECT title FROM issues WHERE title ILIKE '%doc%';
```
```text
            title
------------------------------
 Fix typo in Engine docstring
 Clarify transforms docs
(2 rows)
```

### Limiting

```sql
SELECT number, title FROM issues ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 2;
```

returns the two newest. `LIMIT` with `OFFSET` gives pages, like GitHub's (lesson 4.10 does this properly).

### Counting and summarising

**Aggregate functions** turn many rows into one value:

```sql
SELECT count(*) FROM issues;
SELECT count(*), max(comments), avg(comments) FROM issues WHERE repo = 'pytorch/ignite';
```
```text
 count
-------
     5
(1 row)

 count | max |        avg
-------+-----+--------------------
     4 |   8 | 3.7500000000000000
(1 row)
```

Also `min`, `sum`. Lesson 3.3 groups rows to get one summary per repository.

## UPDATE and DELETE

```sql
UPDATE issues SET state = 'closed' WHERE number = 101;
```
```text
UPDATE 1
```

```sql
DELETE FROM issues WHERE number = 999;
```
```text
DELETE 0
```

The reply says how many rows were affected: always read it. `DELETE 0` means nothing matched: harmless here, but if you expected one row, something's wrong.

**`UPDATE` or `DELETE` without `WHERE` changes every row in the table.** Before running one, run the same `WHERE` as a `SELECT` and check what it returns.

## The database enforces your rules

```sql
INSERT INTO issues (number, repo, title, created_at)
VALUES (101, 'pytorch/ignite', 'Duplicate', now());
```
```text
ERROR:  duplicate key value violates unique constraint "issues_pkey"
DETAIL:  Key (number)=(101) already exists.
```

```sql
INSERT INTO issues (number, repo, created_at) VALUES (106, 'pytorch/ignite', now());
```
```text
ERROR:  null value in column "title" of relation "issues" violates not-null constraint
DETAIL:  Failing row contains (106, pytorch/ignite, null, open, 0, 2026-11-17 17:20:40.306318+00).
```

Read errors the same way as Python tracebacks: what rule (`not-null constraint`), which column (`title`), which data (`DETAIL`). Rules in the database protect your data from *every* program that writes to it, including future ones with bugs. Python checks can be skipped; constraints can't.

(Look closely at the first error. Using the issue number alone as the primary key has a flaw: issue 101 in `pytorch/vision` could never be stored. You'll fix the design in lesson 3.4.)

## Common mistakes

- **Double quotes for text.** `WHERE repo = "pytorch/ignite"` fails: double quotes are for names of columns and tables. Text uses single quotes.
- **`= NULL`** instead of `IS NULL`.
- **`UPDATE`/`DELETE` without `WHERE`.**
- **Relying on row order** without `ORDER BY`.
- **Forgetting the semicolon** in psql: the prompt changes to `atlas-#`, waiting for the rest of the statement. Type `;` and Enter.

## Check yourself

**1.** Write a query for the titles of open issues in `pytorch/ignite` created in 2026, oldest first.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
```sql
SELECT title
FROM issues
WHERE repo = 'pytorch/ignite'
  AND state = 'open'
  AND created_at >= '2026-01-01'
ORDER BY created_at;
```
:::

**2.** An `UPDATE` replies `UPDATE 0`. What does that tell you?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No rows matched the `WHERE` condition, so nothing changed. Usually a wrong value in the condition, or the row doesn't exist.
:::

**3.** Why put `NOT NULL` on `title` when the Python code always sets it?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Because other code (another script, a future feature, a manual fix in psql) can write to the table too, and the Python check doesn't protect against them. The database rule applies to every write, from every client.
:::

## Exercise

In the practice database:

1. Insert two more issues for `pytorch/ignite`, one with 3 comments.
2. Find every issue whose title starts with `Add` or `Support`.
3. Close every `pytorch/ignite` issue with zero comments, checking with a `SELECT` first.
4. Show the number of open issues and the total comments across them.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```sql
INSERT INTO issues (number, repo, title, comments, created_at) VALUES
    (106, 'pytorch/ignite', 'Document the State object', 3, now()),
    (107, 'pytorch/ignite', 'Add type hints to metrics', 0, now());

SELECT number, title FROM issues WHERE title LIKE 'Add%' OR title LIKE 'Support%';

SELECT number FROM issues WHERE repo = 'pytorch/ignite' AND comments = 0;
UPDATE issues SET state = 'closed' WHERE repo = 'pytorch/ignite' AND comments = 0;

SELECT count(*), sum(comments) FROM issues WHERE state = 'open';
```

The `SELECT` before the `UPDATE` uses exactly the same `WHERE`, so you know which rows will change.
:::

## Stretch

Postgres can return the rows an `INSERT`, `UPDATE` or `DELETE` touched, with `RETURNING`. Close issue 102 and get back its number, title and new state in one statement. Why is this useful for an API?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```sql
UPDATE issues SET state = 'closed' WHERE number = 102 RETURNING number, title, state;
```

An API that changes something usually responds with the changed resource. `RETURNING` gets it in the same round trip instead of a second `SELECT`, and it's guaranteed to be exactly the rows that changed.
:::
